nameStory: The Difoliate Orbweaver gets its name from the Latin 'difoliate,' meaning 'two-leaved,' referring to the distinctive leaf-like projections on either side of its abdomen. These spiky bumps make the spider look like it's sprouting tiny leaves, helping it blend in among real foliage. The scientific name 'hamata' means 'hooked,' likely referring to these same curved projections.
description: The Difoliate Orbweaver is a small, uniquely shaped spider that looks like someone stuck two pointed leaves onto its sides. This distinctive orbweaver has a relatively small, compact body with prominent spiky projections extending from either side of its abdomen. It's typically small enough to sit comfortably on a quarter, making it one of the more petite members of the orbweaver family. Like other orbweavers, it builds the classic circular web we all recognize.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Two prominent, leaf-like spikes stick out from either side of the abdomen, giving the spider an unmistakable angular silhouette that feels almost triangular when viewed from above

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds a typical circular orb web with sticky spiral threads, often positioned between shrubs or low vegetation where the spider can blend with surrounding leaves

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and compact, with the body easily fitting on a quarter - the spiky projections make it appear larger than it actually is

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Usually displays muted brown, tan, or greenish coloration that helps it mimic dead or living leaves, with the projections often darker than the main body

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits motionless in or near the center of its web during the day, with its leaf-like projections helping it disappear among real foliage

habitat: Look for Difoliate Orbweavers in shrubby areas, forest edges, and gardens where they can string their webs between low branches and stems. They prefer spots with mixed vegetation where their leaf-like appearance helps them blend in perfectly. You'll often find them in areas with dense undergrowth, particularly around deciduous shrubs and small trees.

seasonality.spring: Adults are rarely seen in early spring, as this species is most active during warmer months when insects are abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for spotting Difoliate Orbweavers, when adults are actively building webs and hunting. Look for their distinctive silhouette in the center of small orb webs.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall, though numbers begin to decline as temperatures drop. Egg-laying typically occurs during this season.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts, surviving the winter only as eggs that will hatch the following warm season.

funFact: This spider is such a master of disguise that it can fool not just predators, but even experienced naturalists - many people walk right past their webs thinking the spider is just a dead leaf caught in the silk!
confusionNotes: The leaf-like projections make this spider nearly impossible to confuse with any other New England orbweaver. If you see those distinctive spiky 'leaves' sticking out from the sides, you've found your Difoliate Orbweaver - no other spider in our region has this feature.
contextualKnowledge: This is the only species in the genus Acacesia found in the United States, making it quite special. While the genus has other members further south into Central and South America, our New England populations represent the northern edge of this spider's range.
compareHints: Since this is the only Acacesia species in North America, it's unique among our orbweavers. Other common orbweavers like the Garden Spider are much larger and lack the distinctive leaf-like projections. The Marbled Orbweaver has an angular abdomen but lacks the prominent spiky projections that make the Difoliate Orbweaver so distinctive.
